PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT

THIS PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT (“Agreement”) is entered into this    day of May, 2024, by and between the City of Westwood, Kansas, a municipal corporation (“City,”) and Columbia Capital Management, LLC, a Missouri limited liability company having its principle place of business in Merriam, Kansas (“Consultant”).

WHEREAS, the City needs professional assistance to perform the services outlined in the Scope of Services described in Exhibit A; and

WHEREAS, the Consultant represents that it has sufficient experience and qualified personnel to perform the professional services herein described on behalf of the City; and

WHEREAS, The City has determined, based upon information provided by the Consultant, that Consultant is qualified to provide the professional services described herein.

WHEREAS, the City and Consultant desire to enter into this Agreement to set forth the specific terms and conditions of their relationship.

NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants, promises, and agreements set forth herein, the parties agree as follows:

clause_units.clause_unit_entire_text:
SECTION 2. Services.

Scope of Services. Consultant shall perform those services (“Contract Services”) described under Scope of Services in Exhibit A, which is attached to this Agreement and incorporated herein by reference. The City may also request additional services not anticipated at the time of this Agreement. At the City’s request, the Consultant shall submit a written scope of the additional work including an estimate of additional costs for the performance of the additional work. No change in scope shall be effective nor additional compensation be paid, except on the basis of the provisions of a written supplemental agreement or an amendment signed by the Parties.

Subcontracting Services. Consultant may not, without first obtaining the City’s written consent, subcontract any of the Contract Services. Notwithstanding the City’s consent to any subcontracting, Consultant shall remain fully responsible for all obligations under this Agreement.

Time of Performance. The Consultant agrees to complete the Contract Services within the times listed in Exhibit A, Scope of Service. In absence of written directions to the contrary, receipt of the executed Agreement shall be the Consultant’s Notice to Proceed. At the City’s discretion, an extension of time may be granted to the  Consultant for delays determined by the City as unavoidable. Consultant may request an extension of time stating the reasons for such a request. The term of this Agreement may be extended by mutual agreement of the parties beyond the time periods outlined in Exhibit A for the purpose of the Consultant providing any additional services, as outlined in Exhibit A, as may be requested by City and agreed to by Consultant. The Parties agree that time for performance of the Contract Services is of the essence and that the Consultant’s failure to meet the contractual times for performance shall constitute a material breach of this Agreement.

Qualified Personnel. Consultant shall provide sufficient qualified personnel to perform the Contract Services. If directed by the City, the Consultant shall remove any person the Consultant employs in connection with the work.

Performance. In performing the Contract Services, Consultant agrees to take all steps necessary for the full and effective performance of those tasks.

Assistance from City. To assist Consultant in performing the Contract Services, the City will perform the duties outlined in Exhibit A, if any, in a timely manner so as not to unreasonably delay the Consultant’s services.

explanation_call.reason: As currently drafted, the City may terminate this Agreement for "cause" with the same sixty (60) days' notice used for a convenience termination, without any obligation to identify the alleged breach or afford Columbia Capital Management an opportunity to remedy it. This exposes Columbia Capital Management to the reputational and financial consequences of a for-cause termination — which may trigger downstream rights or affect future engagements — without any procedural safeguard against an erroneous or disputed allegation. The absence of a cure period also means that a minor, readily correctable performance issue could be weaponized to terminate the relationship on a "cause" basis rather than for convenience, with no practical distinction in outcome for Columbia Capital Management. Additionally, while sixty (60) days' notice is stated, the clause does not expressly fix the effective date of termination by reference to delivery of that notice, creating potential ambiguity about when Columbia Capital Management's obligations and payment entitlements cease.
explanation_call.suggested_fix: SECTION 4. Termination of Agreement. The City may terminate this Agreement at any time on and after November 30, 2024, for convenience upon sixty (60) days' written notice to Consultant, effective sixty (60) days following delivery of such notice. The City may terminate this Agreement for cause upon written notice to Consultant specifying the material breach in reasonable detail, provided that Consultant shall have thirty (30) days following delivery of such notice to cure the identified breach, and termination for cause shall not take effect if Consultant cures the breach within that period. If the City terminates the Agreement under this Section, the City shall pay the Consultant for Contract Services satisfactorily performed by Consultant before the effective date of termination, and for all associated expenses incurred by the Consultant before the termination. Under no circumstances will the Consultant be entitled to anticipatory profits or consequential damages. Consultant may terminate the agreement at any time upon sixty (60) days' written notice, effective sixty (60) days following delivery of such notice. The provisions regarding indemnity and insurance shall survive the termination of this Agreement.

Under no circumstances will the Consultant be entitled to anticipatory profits or consequential damages. Consultant may terminate the agreement at any time upon sixty (60) days’ written notice. The provisions regarding indemnity and insurance shall survive the termination of this Agreement.

Let me re-read.

The clause says "The City may terminate this Agreement" and "Consultant may terminate the agreement." The agreement is a Professional Services Agreement. Columbia Capital Management would be the Consultant providing services to the City. Let me evaluate from that perspective.
For TER-01, the City can terminate "for convenience or cause," giving two distinct grounds, while the Consultant can terminate with 60 days' notice without specified grounds. The question is whether "cause" satisfies the "material breach" requirement, since the two terms aren't identical though cause often encompasses breach.

I'll settle on Partly met for this criterion since neither ground named is specifically "material breach."

Looking at suspension (TER-06), the clause doesn't address this, so it's not applicable. explanation_thinking_by_para.A6D7967B:
Let me analyze the issues identified:

1. Grounds for termination - partly met: The City can terminate for convenience or cause, but "cause" is not defined. Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant) needs clarity on what constitutes "cause" and what rights they have when terminated for cause vs. convenience.

2. No cure period for breach - not met: There is no opportunity to remedy a breach before termination. This is critical for Columbia Capital Management as the Consultant - if the City terminates for cause (breach), Columbia Capital Management should have an opportunity to cure before termination takes effect.

3. Written notice and when termination takes effect - partly met: The 60-day notice is stated for both parties, but the City's termination clause redundantly says "written notice" twice ("sixty (60) days' written notice for convenience or cause upon written notice to Consultant"), which is awkward. More critically, the effective date of termination is not explicitly stated (is it 60 days after the notice? The clause implies this but doesn't say it clearly).

From Columbia Capital Management's standpoint, the absence of a cure period is the biggest exposure: the City could invoke "cause" without any chance to fix the alleged issue, which matters since cause vs. convenience could affect their standing even though the payment clause fortunately covers work performed under either scenario. The key fix needed is building in a cure period before cause-based termination takes effect.

I'm drafting a surgical revision adding a 30-day cure window after written notice specifying the breach, plus clarifying that termination is effective 60 days after notice, keeping the revised section comparable in length to the original.

For the explanation, I need to name Columbia Capital Management specifically, highlight the risk of lacking a cure period, and flag that "cause" is undefined—while noting the survival clause is less critical to address since it's already covered.

suggestions.reason: As currently drafted, the City may terminate this Agreement for "cause" with the same sixty (60) days' notice used for a convenience termination, without any obligation to identify the alleged breach or afford Columbia Capital Management an opportunity to remedy it. This exposes Columbia Capital Management to the reputational and financial consequences of a for-cause termination — which may trigger downstream rights or affect future engagements — without any procedural safeguard against an erroneous or disputed allegation. The absence of a cure period also means that a minor, readily correctable performance issue could be weaponized to terminate the relationship on a "cause" basis rather than for convenience, with no practical distinction in outcome for Columbia Capital Management. Additionally, while sixty (60) days' notice is stated, the clause does not expressly fix the effective date of termination by reference to delivery of that notice, creating potential ambiguity about when Columbia Capital Management's obligations and payment entitlements cease.

That matters because it means both the compliance obligation and indemnification obligation fall solely on Columbia Capital Management as Consultant, with no reciprocal duties on the City's side - so for CMP-01, compliance with laws is only "partly met" since it's one-sided.

SECTION 8. Insurance.

General. Consultant shall secure and maintain, throughout the duration of this Agreement, insurance (on an occurrence basis unless otherwise agreed in writing) of such types and in at least such amounts as required herein. The City shall be named as  an additional insured for all coverages required herein except workers’ compensation coverage and professional liability coverage. All insurance procured for this Agreement by the Consultant, including additional insured designations, shall be primary and noncontributory. Consultant shall provide certificates of insurance on forms acceptable to the City at the time of this Agreement’s execution. The Certificate shall specify the date when such insurance expires. A renewal certificate shall be furnished to the City before the expiration date of any coverage. The City shall be notified by receipt of written notice from the insurer at least 30 days before material modification or cancellation of any policy listed on the Certificate.

Notice of Claim. Consultant, upon receiving notice of any claim in connection with this Agreement, shall promptly notify the City, providing full details thereof, including an estimate of the amount of loss or liability.

Reduction of Policy Limits. Consultant shall monitor and promptly notify the City of any reduction in limits of protection afforded under any policy listed in the Certificate (or otherwise required by this Agreement) if the Consultant’s limits of protection have been impaired or reduced to such extent that the limits fall below the minimum amounts required hereunder. In that event, Consultant shall promptly reinstate the original limits of liability required hereunder and shall furnish evidence thereof to the City.

Industry Ratings. Consultant agrees that its insurance carrier must:

a. Be licensed to do business in the State of Kansas;

b. Carry a Best’s policyholder rating of “A-” or better and;

c. Carry at least a Class VIII financial rating; OR

Be acceptable to the City.

Insurance Required. Consultant agrees to secure and maintain the following insurance:

Commercial General Liability. Consultant shall maintain General Liability coverage including Premises-Operations Liability, Independent Contractors Liability, Products and Completed Operations, and Broad Form Property Damage within these minimum limits:

Bodily Injury & Property Damage	$1,000,000 combined single limit per occurrence: $2,000,000 annual aggregate

Fire Damage Liability	$50,000

Medical Payments	$5,000

The property damage liability coverage shall contain no exclusion relative to blasting, explosion, collapse of buildings, or damages to underground property.

Comprehensive Automobile Liability. Consultant shall maintain Automobile Liability coverage including coverage for Owned, Hired and Non-owned Auto Liability providing for all injuries to members of the public and damage to property of others arising from the use of motor vehicles on and off the Work site with these minimum limits:

Bodily Injury & Property Damage	$1,000,000 combined single limit per occurrence

Workers’ Compensation and Employer’s Liability. Consultant shall maintain Workers’ Compensation coverage for all claims made under applicable state workers’ compensation laws. Consultant shall also maintain Employer’s Liability coverage for claims made for injury, disease, or death of an employee that, for any reason, may not fall within the provisions of a workers’ compensation law. The following minimum limits shall apply:

Workers’ Compensation	Statutory Limits

Employers’ Liability	$500,000 each accident; $500,000 disease – policy limit; $500,000 disease – each employee

Professional Liability Insurance. Consultant shall maintain Professional Liability Insurance in an amount of no less than $1,000,000.

Subcontractor’s Insurance. If a part of this Agreement is to be sublet, the Consultant shall either:

Cover all subcontractors under its insurance policies; or

Require each subcontractor not so covered to secure insurance that will protect subcontractor against all applicable hazards or risks of loss as and in the minimum amounts designated.

Whichever option is chosen, Consultant shall indemnify and hold harmless the City as to any and all damages, claims, or losses, including attorneys’ fees, arising out of or resulting from the acts or omissions of its subcontractors.

explanation_call.reason: The savings clause preserving duties "as imposed by law" is undefined and open-ended, meaning that despite the no-third-party-beneficiary restriction, the clause expressly leaves intact every statutory and common law obligation either party owes to third parties without qualification or ceiling. For Columbia Capital Management, this creates a material financial risk: a third party who cannot sue under the Agreement could nonetheless argue that this clause confirms the survival of unlimited tort, statutory, or regulatory duties owed by Columbia Capital Management, potentially bypassing any liability cap negotiated elsewhere in the Agreement. The phrase "as imposed by law" is sufficiently indeterminate that two courts could read it to preserve materially different categories of third-party liability, leaving Columbia Capital Management's exposure scope unresolved at the moment a claim arises. Anchoring the savings clause to "applicable law" and expressly subordinating preserved duties to the Agreement's limitation of liability provisions closes this gap.

Let me analyze the survivorship clause (Section 27) against each criterion from Columbia Capital Management's perspective.

The clause reads: "Notwithstanding the termination of this Agreement, Consultant's obligations with respect to Insurance (Section 8) and Indemnification (Section 9), and any other terms and conditions that by their nature should survive termination, shall survive the termination of this Agreement."

Let me evaluate each criterion:

**GEN-01: One-sided obligations?**
The survivorship clause only mentions "Consultant's obligations" surviving - specifically Insurance (Section 8) and Indemnification (Section 9). It doesn't mention any of the City's (or counterparty's) corresponding obligations surviving. 

If Columbia Capital Management is the Consultant here, this one-sidedness favors them negatively - only their obligations survive, with no mention of surviving rights like payment or IP ownership, though the catch-all language for terms that "by their nature should survive" could pull in some bilateral protections. I'm also pausing to consider whether Columbia Capital Management is actually the Consultant or the City in this agreement, since that determines whether this asymmetry helps or hurts their position.

The clause itself doesn't create new financial obligations, just preserves existing ones referenced elsewhere. The phrase "by their nature should survive termination" is vague and undefined, though courts typically interpret such language contextually. More concerning is that surviving indemnification obligations could expose Columbia Capital Management to unlimited post-termination liability if Section 9 lacks a cap or time limit.

The clause also only preserves the Consultant's obligations without mentioning corresponding post-termination rights like final payment or property retrieval, creating an unpaired obligation. No placeholders or contradictions appear, but the ambiguity around "by their nature" remains a genuine point lawyers could dispute, while the termination trigger itself is clearly defined.

Running through the final determinations: survivorship is only partly met since rights aren't expressly preserved, vague time standards aren't an issue in the operative clause itself, there's no new financial obligation created here, and the undefined catch-all phrase along with unlimited indemnification exposure both represent partial compliance concerns worth flagging.

thinking_trace.extraction_thinking:
Let me analyze the clause text carefully against each criterion from Columbia Capital Management's perspective (the Consultant/reviewed party).

The clause text is from Exhibit A: Scope of Services, specifically about the Appointment of Consultant. Let me identify the parties:
- The City = client/appointing party
- Consultant = Columbia Capital Management (the reviewed party)

Let me evaluate each criterion:

**GEN-01: One-sided obligations**
The clause appoints the Consultant and states that "By accepting such appointment, Consultant agrees that at all times it shall act in accordance with the terms and conditions of this Agreement and all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking." 

This is somewhat one-sided - the Consultant accepts obligations ("at all times it shall act in accordance with...all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking") while the City simply "appoints" without corresponding obligations being stated here. 

That broad phrase about "all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" could expose Columbia to open-ended legal obligations, though this is standard for an appointment clause, so I'll call it partly met.

For GEN-02, there's no vague time standard here since "at all times" is a continuing duty rather than a deadline, so this is likely not applicable or met. GEN-03 doesn't apply either since there are no financial amounts or caps referenced in this provision. Now I'm checking GEN-04 for any undefined terms that could create ambiguity.

"Accounts" is defined broadly in the clause itself, covering idle funds, cash, deposits, investments, capital accounts, and bond proceeds, but terms like "investment adviser," "investment management," and "provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" are left undefined or only loosely tied to regulatory meaning. That broad compliance language, paired with the sweeping scope of managed assets, raises a real concern under GEN-05 for unlimited liability exposure.

No unfilled placeholders are visible, so GEN-06 is met. I don't see any internal contradictions either, though I can't check this clause against the rest of the agreement, so GEN-07 is tentatively met based on available text. For GEN-08, the City gains investment management services while Columbia Capital Management gains the appointment and broad compliance duties, but there's no corresponding obligation from the City in this clause, so that imbalance stands. On GEN-09, the phrase "all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" remains a significant ambiguity, alongside the sweeping scope of what counts as pooled cash under management.

Finalizing my assessments now: the clause is partly compliant across several criteria -- the obligations run one-directionally against the Consultant with undefined legal scope, undefined terms around "this undertaking," potentially unlimited liability exposure with no cap, and unpaired rights since the Consultant's duties aren't matched by stated compensation or protection terms in this clause. GEN-02, GEN-06, GEN-07, and GEN-10 are fully met, while GEN-03 doesn't apply since no financial figures appear here.

explanation_thinking_by_para.A09DE6DB:
Let me analyze this carefully.

The key issues are:
1. One-sided obligations - only the Consultant (Columbia Capital Management) has compliance obligations; the City has no corresponding obligations
2. "All other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" is undefined and vague - creates open-ended and potentially unlimited compliance obligations
3. Unlimited/uncapped liability exposure through "at all times" + "all other provisions of law" - any breach of any law could constitute a contract breach
4. Ambiguity - "provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" is so broad two lawyers would read it differently

Columbia Capital Management is the Consultant here. The City is appointing them.

The fix should:
narrow that vague catch-all phrase to something more defined like applicable federal, state, and local laws governing investment advisory services, possibly add a materiality qualifier to cap the exposure, and introduce a reciprocal obligation requiring the City to cooperate or comply with applicable law in connection with its own duties under the Agreement. I'm drafting the specific replacement language now.

The real fix is narrowing "all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" to "all applicable laws and regulations governing investment advisory services" plus adding "in all material respects" as a qualifier, and I should also add a reciprocal City obligation to provide necessary information. I'm now drafting the revised appointment clause with these changes worked in.

suggestions.reason: The compliance covenant imposed on Columbia Capital Management through the phrase "all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking" is undefined, unbounded, and potentially unlimited in scope, exposing Columbia Capital Management to breach of contract liability for any failure to comply with any law across any conceivable legal framework — a standard no reasonable counterparty counsel would accept and no court could apply with certainty. The absence of a materiality qualifier compounds this exposure, meaning a technical or immaterial regulatory deviation could be characterised as a breach of the Agreement, triggering remedies against Columbia Capital Management with no proportionality check. Additionally, the clause imposes compliance obligations exclusively on Columbia Capital Management while placing no corresponding obligation on the City to cooperate, provide accurate information, or fulfill its own duties in connection with the Accounts. These defects should be addressed before execution, as the appointment clause is foundational and cross-references to any indemnification or termination provisions in the Agreement may amplify Columbia Capital Management's exposure under the current formulation.
suggestions.original_text: Appointment of Consultant. The City hereby appoints Consultant to act as the investment adviser and to assume the responsibilities of investment management of the pooled cash of the City including all idle funds, cash, deposits, investments, capital accounts and bond proceeds (the “Accounts”). Consultant does hereby accept said appointment as an investment adviser under the Accounts. By accepting such appointment, Consultant agrees that at all times it shall act in accordance with the terms and conditions of this Agreement and all other provisions of law applicable to this undertaking.

Let me analyze this clause carefully against each criterion from Columbia Capital Management's perspective as the client being represented.

The clause is about fiduciary duties imposed on the Consultant. Columbia Capital Management is the client/customer receiving services. The Consultant is managing assets for Columbia Capital Management.

Let me evaluate each criterion:

**GEN-01: One-sided obligations**
The clause imposes fiduciary duties on the Consultant (not Columbia Capital Management). This is actually beneficial to Columbia Capital Management as the client. The obligations run from Consultant to Columbia Capital Management. However, the prudent person standard ("prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters") is somewhat vague. From Columbia Capital Management's perspective, this is actually favorable - it imposes obligations on the Consultant. But there's no corresponding obligation on Columbia Capital Management. 

Reconsidering this - since Columbia Capital Management is the client, obligations placed on the Consultant actually protect and advantage Columbia Capital Management rather than disadvantage it, so this criterion appears to be satisfied.

**GEN-02: Vague time standards**
I'm now checking whether the clause specifies concrete time periods or relies on vague language instead.

"Assets it manages pursuant to this Agreement" could use a clearer reference to a schedule, but "prudent person" and "enterprise of like character" are established legal terms of art. I'll lean toward Met since these terms carry recognized commercial/legal meaning even if the specific asset scope isn't pinned down here. Moving to GEN-05, the clause establishes a fiduciary duty that could create exposure for unlimited liability.

But thinking it through, this standard creates obligations on the Consultant, not unlimited liability for Columbia Capital Management, so I'll mark it Met. GEN-06 has no placeholders visible, so Met. GEN-07 shows no internal contradictions and there's nothing else in the batch to compare against, so Met. For GEN-08, the clause imposes fiduciary obligations on the Consultant but doesn't explicitly state Columbia Capital Management's right to enforce them or remedies for breach, though equitable remedies for fiduciary breaches are generally implied, making this somewhat incomplete.

I'm settling on Partly Met for GEN-08 since the obligation runs favorably toward Columbia Capital Management but the corresponding enforcement right isn't spelled out. For GEN-09, the prudent person standard is well-established and the "in addition to, but not in lieu of" language is clear, but phrases like "assets it manages pursuant to this Agreement" and "enterprise of like character and with like aims" introduce some subjectivity, so I'm leaning Partly Met. Moving to GEN-10, I'm looking at what conditions trigger the fiduciary obligation.

"enterprise of like character and with like aims" is vague, since GEN-05 through GEN-10 mostly look satisfied - no unlimited liability, no placeholders, no contradictions, but GEN-08 lacks explicit remedies for breach of fiduciary duty and GEN-09 has that same ambiguous "like character" phrasing. explanation_thinking_by_para.BF539E01:
Let me analyze the issues with this fiduciary clause from Columbia Capital Management's perspective.

The issues are:
1. Undefined terms - "a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in an enterprise of like character and with like aims" - this is actually the ERISA prudent person/expert standard language, but "enterprise of like character and with like aims" is vague
2. One-sided clause - imposes obligations on Consultant without corresponding remedies for Columbia Capital Management
3. Ambiguity - "enterprise of like character and with like aims" is vague

The clause is based on ERISA's prudent expert standard (29 U.S.C. 1104(a)(1)(B)), using this exact statutory phrasing, but without defining the comparable "enterprise" in context, Consultant could argue for a lower standard. The clause also lacks any remedy provision for breach of this fiduciary duty, and I need to fix both the definitional gap and the missing enforcement mechanism.

My fix anchors the undefined "enterprise of like character and with like aims" to the specific investment management context, replacing it with language like "an investment management enterprise of like character and with similar investment objectives" so Consultant can't point to lower-standard comparators outside this field.

suggestions.reason: The clause imposes a fiduciary duty on Consultant using language that mirrors ERISA's prudent-person standard, but the phrases "enterprise of like character and with like aims" are entirely undefined and unanchored within the Agreement, leaving the operative benchmark open to dispute. If Consultant were to breach its fiduciary obligations, it could invoke a comparator enterprise with materially lower standards than the investment management mandate actually entrusted to Consultant under this Agreement, diluting the protection Columbia Capital Management bargained for. Additionally, the clause is structurally one-sided: it articulates Consultant's duty but provides no express remedy or reference to Consultant's accountability to Columbia Capital Management upon a breach of that standard, leaving Columbia Capital Management to rely solely on general contract law remedies rather than the heightened standard the clause purports to establish.
suggestions.original_text: Fiduciary. In addition to, but not in lieu of any and all applicable fiduciary standards imposed under federal or state law, Consultant shall act as a fiduciary with respect to the assets it manages pursuant to this Agreement. As a fiduciary, Consultant shall perform its duties under this Agreement with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in an enterprise of like character and with like aims.
suggestions.suggested_fix: Fiduciary. In addition to, but not in lieu of any and all applicable fiduciary standards imposed under federal or state law, Consultant shall act as a fiduciary with respect to the assets it manages pursuant to this Agreement. As a fiduciary, Consultant shall perform its duties under this Agreement with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent investment professional acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in an investment management enterprise of like character and with investment objectives similar to those described in this Agreement. Any failure by Consultant to satisfy this standard of care shall constitute a material breach of this Agreement for which Columbia Capital Management shall be entitled to pursue all available remedies.

clause_units.clause_unit_entire_text:
Investment Management Services.

Consultant’s scope of services shall include:

Providing recommendations to the City regarding updating, developing and maintaining an investment policy for the City, consistent with various Kansas statutes pertaining to deposits, investments and collateral management. Philosophically, the City’s investments will be evaluated for safety, liquidity and yield, in that order, with the recognition that ensuring adequate liquidity is also often the best way to preserve principal (safety).

Implementing an investment strategy that allocates the City’s pooled cash into multiple subportfolios with the investments in each subportfolio targeted to the unique needs for and statutory constraints on those subportfolios. Subordinate to the core investment goals of preserving principal and providing adequate liquidity, Consultant shall seek to maximize income from the portfolio that the City can use to support its operations.

Complying with Kansas the requirements of K.S.A. 12-1675 et seq. providing local banks with a “first look” at the City’s investment opportunities where required.

Monitoring and marking-to-market the collateral posted by the City’s bank depositories on a weekly basis to ensure compliance with state law and City policy.

Selecting investment securities for the City’s portfolio, consistent with state law and the City’s investment policy.

Providing periodic portfolio reporting to the City, including information on holdings, transactions, portfolio income and performance.

Working with the city attorney to draft an ordinance designating certain of the City’s funds as multi-year capital funds.

Providing the City with general market information, ad hoc reporting and other routine requests related to investment management.

Consultant shall invest and otherwise manage the assets held by the City, its banks and any Custodian in the Accounts. Responsibility for the investment and management is assigned to Consultant by the City. Consultant shall have sole discretion with respect to investment of funds in the Accounts without prior consultation with the City; however, Consultant shall be bound by such written investment policy objectives and guidelines for the management of the assets as shall from time to time be provided to Consultant by the City. Consultant shall have the authority to select the brokerage firms, consistent with the requirements of K.S.A. 12-1675(b)(4), through which orders will be placed. Consultant may combine orders for the Accounts with orders for other accounts or funds under management. Consultant shall effect all purchases and sales of securities in a manner consistent with the principles of best execution, taking into account net price (including commissions) and execution capability and other services that the broker or dealer may provide. Consultant shall use investment strategies designed to ensure that all securities transactions are executed in such a manner that the total explicit and implicit costs and total proceeds in every transaction are the most favorable under the circumstances. Consultant shall issue suitable instructions to the Custodian with respect to deliveries and payments.

explanation_thinking_by_para.8F455969:
Let me analyze the issue here. The problem is that the scope of services clause is one-sided in a way that disadvantages Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant/client being represented). The scope is very broad and open-ended, with obligations like "other routine requests" and "ad hoc reporting" that create unlimited, undefined service obligations without corresponding limitations or protections.

Key issues:
1. The scope includes "other routine requests" - this is unbounded and could expose Columbia Capital Management to unlimited service demands without additional compensation
2. "Ad hoc reporting" - similarly unbounded
3. No limitation on scope creep or mechanism for addressing out-of-scope requests
4. The obligations are entirely one-sided - all duties flow to the Consultant (Columbia Capital Management) with no reciprocal obligations on the City
5. I want a minimal, surgical fix that adds a reasonableness or frequency qualifier to the "ad hoc reporting and other routine requests" language -- maybe "as mutually agreed" -- to curb scope creep while keeping the rest of the clause intact.
explanation_thinking_by_para.1EA19029:
Let me analyze the clause carefully.

**Original Paragraph:**
"Providing periodic portfolio reporting to the City, including information on holdings, transactions, portfolio income and performance."

**Issues Identified:**
1. Vague time standards - "periodic portfolio reporting" is not anchored to a specific frequency or timeline
2. Ambiguity - "periodic" and the scope of reporting could be interpreted differently by reasonable lawyers

**Client:** Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant/service provider)

**Risk Analysis:**
- "Periodic" is entirely undefined and could be interpreted by the City as requiring very frequent reporting (daily, weekly), imposing an open-ended, undefined operational burden on Columbia Capital Management
- Without a defined frequency, the City could claim insufficient reporting, exposing Columbia Capital Management to breach claims if its cadence falls short of unstated expectations

explanation_thinking_by_para.00C727EF:
Let me analyze the issues identified and draft a focused, surgical finding for Columbia Capital Management.

Key issues:
1. "Best execution" is undefined - leaves its meaning open to dispute
2. "Sole discretion" creates unlimited/uncapped liability exposure for Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant) - without any corresponding right to reject or seek clarification on investment policy guidelines
3. The contradiction between "sole discretion without prior consultation" and being "bound by written investment policy objectives...as shall from time to time be provided" - the City can unilaterally change guidelines without notice period or process
4. One-sided obligation: Consultant is bound by guidelines provided "from time to time" with no corresponding obligation on the City to provide timely, clear, written guidelines before they take effect
5. There's no clarity on when guidelines take effect or what notice is required, which means Columbia Capital Management could face liability for breaching guidelines it never had adequate notice of - compounding the undefined "best execution" standard and the unlimited liability exposure from "sole discretion."

Fixes I'd suggest: define "best execution" against an objective standard, require advance written notice (say, 10 Business Days) before new guidelines take effect, protect Consultant from liability for transactions compliant at the time they were made, and clarify that the "sole discretion" grant operates within the bounds of the guidelines rather than contradicting them.

I'll continue the draft: Consultant acts without prior consultation but remains bound by written guidelines the City provides with ten days' notice, with no liability for trades conforming to guidelines in effect at execution time. I'll add broker selection authority tied to K.S.A. 12-1675(b)(4), ability to combine orders across accounts, and a best-execution standard referencing applicable securities law while weighing net price, execution capability, and other broker services.

suggestions.reason: As currently drafted, the scope of services imposed on Columbia Capital Management is entirely open-ended: the catch-all obligation to respond to "ad hoc reporting and other routine requests" creates an unbounded service obligation with no frequency cap, materiality threshold, or mechanism to treat out-of-scope demands as additional compensable work. This exposes Columbia Capital Management to unlimited service creep at the City's discretion without any corresponding reciprocal commitment from the City to provide timely, accurate information necessary for Columbia Capital Management to perform. Left unaddressed, the City could characterize virtually any request as "routine," effectively expanding Columbia Capital Management's contracted workload without additional compensation or scope adjustment.

suggestions.reason: The clause exposes Columbia Capital Management to two compounding risks. First, the City retains unilateral authority to impose new written investment policy objectives and guidelines "from time to time" with no advance notice period, meaning Columbia Capital Management could be held in breach of guidelines it had no reasonable opportunity to operationalize — creating open-ended liability for prior compliant transactions that post-dated a guideline change. Second, the obligation to achieve "best execution" is left undefined within the clause and apparently nowhere else in the Agreement, creating an ambiguous performance standard against which Columbia Capital Management's execution decisions could be measured retroactively and arbitrarily. Together, these provisions leave Columbia Capital Management operating under a shifting and undefined compliance framework with no corresponding protection for transactions executed in good faith under the guidelines and standards then in effect.

explanation_call.reason: The word "Timely" imposes no objectively enforceable deadline on the City, meaning Columbia Capital Management cannot establish a breach even if critical account data is withheld for weeks, directly undermining its ability to execute and monitor the investment plan. Timely provide Consultant with balances, account statements and interest earned on the City’s funds and accounts.

thinking_trace.extraction_thinking:
Let me analyze this clause carefully against each criterion from the perspective of Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant/reviewed party).

The clause is about custodian instructions - the City shall instruct the Custodian to deliver securities sold and pay for securities purchased, including expenses, in accordance with confirmations provided by the Consultant.

Let me evaluate each criterion:

**GEN-01: One-sided obligations**
The clause places an obligation on the City (not on Columbia Capital Management/Consultant). The City must instruct the Custodian. The Consultant provides confirmations. This seems relatively balanced or even favorable to the Consultant - the City bears the obligation. However, from Columbia Capital Management's perspective, the clause places the burden of providing "copies of confirmations" on the Consultant, without any obligation on the City or Custodian to act within a specified timeframe. 

Looking closer, the clause requires CCM to provide confirmations without any corresponding obligation on the City/Custodian to act timely, but the main operative obligation is still on the City to instruct the Custodian. Since CCM's burden is comparatively minor, I lean toward this criterion being Met.

**GEN-02: Vague time standards**
No time standards appear in this clause at all - nothing specifies when the City must instruct the Custodian or when delivery/payment must occur. Since the obligation is inherently time-sensitive but no definite period is stated, this leans toward Not met, though the criterion is really aimed at vague terms like "promptly" rather than complete silence.

**GEN-03: Financial amounts**
The clause references expenses like brokerage commissions and transfer taxes without giving specific amounts or formulas, which is typical since these depend on actual transactions rather than fixed figures. Since no amounts or formulas are specified for these expenses, I'll mark this as Not met, though the actual financial terms would presumably be determined by the transaction confirmations.

**GEN-04: Undefined terms**
"Custodian" and "Consultant" are likely defined elsewhere, and "K.S.A. 12-1675(e)(1)" is a Kansas statute reference rather than a contractual term, but "confirmations" lacks a clear definition despite being a standard securities term. I'll call this Partly met given that most terms probably have adequate definitions except for this one.

**GEN-05: Unlimited liability**
This clause places an obligation on the City rather than creating liability for Columbia Capital Management, so no unlimited liability issue arises here - Met.

**GEN-06 through GEN-09**
I see no unfilled placeholders and no contradictions within this single clause, so those are Met. There's a slight imbalance though: the obligation on the City to instruct the Custodian based on confirmations from Consultant doesn't come with a corresponding enforcement right for CCM if the City fails to comply, nor any required timeframe for the Custodian to act, making this Partly met. The phrase "copies of confirmations provided to the Custodian by Consultant" also raises ambiguity about format and process that I should flag.

**GEN-10 and final assessment**
The trigger for the City's instruction obligation seems to be an ongoing standing arrangement tied to securities transactions rather than an explicit conditional event, so I'll mark this Partly met. Pulling everything together: GEN-01 Met, GEN-02 Not met since no delivery/payment timing is specified, GEN-03 Met, GEN-04 Partly met due to "confirmations" being undefined, GEN-05 Met since no unlimited liability arises for CCM, GEN-06 and GEN-07 Met, and GEN-08 through GEN-10 Partly met for the reasons above.

explanation_thinking_by_para.33F0E92C:
Let me analyze the clause carefully.

**Original Paragraph:**
"Custodian. Pursuant to K.S.A. 12-1675(e)(1) the City shall instruct the Custodian to deliver securities sold and pay for securities purchased, including all expenses relating to the purchase and sale of such securities, such as brokerage commissions and transfer taxes, in accordance with copies of confirmations provided to the Custodian by Consultant."

**Issues identified:**
1. One-sided obligations - the City's obligation to instruct the Custodian is entirely dependent on "confirmations provided to the Custodian by Consultant" but there's no obligation on Consultant (Columbia Capital Management) to actually provide those confirmations in a timely manner.
2. There's no stated timeframe for Consultant to deliver confirmations or for the City to then instruct the Custodian, and "copies of confirmations" is left undefined -- it's unclear what form or content qualifies, creating a vague condition precedent that favors Columbia Capital Management without a matching obligation.

For Columbia specifically, this delay risk cuts both ways: if the City drags on instructing the Custodian after receiving confirmations, trades could fail to settle, exposing Columbia to settlement risk and potential losses from undefined timing obligations.

I should fix this by adding a specific timeframe, like requiring the City to instruct the Custodian within one business day of receiving written trade confirmations, and clarifying that those confirmations are the trigger for settlement instructions. I'm drafting language citing K.S.A. 12-1675(e)(1) that ties the City's instruction obligation to receipt of written confirmations from the Consultant.

explanation_call.suggested_fix: Potential Conflicts of Consultant. explanation_call.reason: As currently drafted, this clause imposes a unilateral disclosure obligation exclusively on Columbia Capital Management as Consultant, while placing no corresponding notice obligation on the City regarding events that may equally affect the Accounts or Columbia Capital Management's ability to perform its obligations. This asymmetry leaves Columbia Capital Management operationally exposed: if the City becomes aware of a material event pertaining to the Accounts but has no contractual duty to disclose it, Columbia Capital Management may be left without information critical to managing those Accounts and could face liability for decisions made in ignorance. The undefined scope of "certain events" further compounds this risk, as it creates ambiguity about whether Columbia Capital Management has fully discharged its notice obligation, potentially exposing it to breach claims by the City.

thinking_trace.extraction_thinking:
Let me analyze this clause carefully against each criterion from the perspective of Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant).

The clause reads: "Proxy Voting. The City shall direct the Custodian in voting of all proxies and Consultant shall have no responsibility in respect of the voting of proxies."

This is a proxy voting clause in a Professional Services Agreement where Columbia Capital Management appears to be the "Consultant" and the other party is "The City."

Let me evaluate each criterion:

**GEN-01: One-sided obligations**
The clause assigns proxy voting direction entirely to The City and completely absolves the Consultant (Columbia Capital Management) of any responsibility. From Columbia Capital Management's perspective as the Consultant, this is actually favorable - it removes responsibility from them. 

Since the obligation falls on The City rather than CCM, this works in CCM's favor, so I'd call this Met. For GEN-02, there's no time-sensitive language at all, so that's Not Applicable, and similarly GEN-03 has no financial amounts or caps, also Not Applicable. Looking at GEN-04, "Custodian" appears to be a capitalized defined term established elsewhere in the agreement, while "proxies" carries a standard commercial meaning.

For GEN-05, the clause actually relieves Columbia Capital Management of responsibility for proxy voting, which protects rather than burdens them, so that's Met. No placeholders or contradictions are visible, so GEN-06 and GEN-07 are both Met. On GEN-08, while The City bears the obligation to direct the Custodian without a reciprocal obligation from the Consultant, this asymmetry actually favors CCM since it shields them from liability rather than disadvantaging them.

For GEN-09, the ambiguity question seems fine since "no responsibility in respect of the voting of proxies" is clear enough - Met. GEN-10 also seems satisfied since the obligation on The City appears standing and continuous without needing a specific trigger.

Revisiting GEN-01 though, I want to push harder on CCM's advocacy angle: the clause entirely strips CCM of any role, right, or advisory capacity in proxy voting, which as a capital management consultant they might reasonably want some say in.

Actually, reconsidering from a liability standpoint, this exclusion protects CCM rather than harming them - so GEN-01 should be Met, not flagged as one-sided. For GEN-08, I'm settling on Partly Met since The City holds the exclusive obligation and right to direct proxies while CCM has none at all, which creates some imbalance even though CCM benefits from reduced responsibility.

For GEN-10, I'm thinking through whether these proxy obligations are conditional - they seem to be standing obligations that apply continuously whenever proxy votes occur, rather than being triggered by a specific milestone, so this should be Not Applicable.

explanation_thinking_by_para.C9005322:
Let me analyze the clause carefully:

**Original Paragraph Text:**
"Proxy Voting. The City shall direct the Custodian in voting of all proxies and Consultant shall have no responsibility in respect of the voting of proxies."

**Issues identified:**
1. "Custodian" is not defined in this clause or apparently in the broader agreement, leaving its meaning open to dispute.
2. The City has the obligation to direct the Custodian in proxy voting, but the Consultant's exclusion from responsibility is absolute and unqualified - there's no corresponding obligation on the Consultant to provide recommendations or guidance if requested, nor is there a right for Columbia Capital Management (the Consultant) to offer proxy voting recommendations.
3. The phrase "no responsibility" is ambiguous - it could mean no duty to vote, no liability for voting outcomes, or no involvement whatsoever including providing recommendations.

For Columbia Capital Management as Consultant, this broad waiver is mostly protective, but the ambiguity cuts both ways - a narrow reading preserves their liability shield, while a broad reading could unintentionally restrict their ability to offer input or recommendations, limiting the scope of services they could otherwise provide.

I'm also noting that "Custodian" is left undefined, which creates uncertainty about who actually controls the voting process and whether that party is properly directed under the agreement.

My suggested fix is to clarify that the City directs the custodian holding the Account's assets on proxy voting, while Columbia Capital Management has no duty to vote, direct, or recommend on proxies and bears no liability for voting outcomes - keeping the revision concise and proportionate to the original clause.

"Custodian" is left undefined anywhere in the Agreement, creating ambiguity over which entity the City must direct and whether that direction occurred. Also, "no responsibility in respect of the voting of proxies" is imprecise enough that it could be read as stripping Columbia Capital Management of its right to even offer proxy voting recommendations, which would undercut its advisory mandate and expose it to a claim that silence on a material vote was a breach.

My fix defines "Custodian" explicitly as the entity holding the City's investment assets, and clarifies the exclusion covers both duty to vote and liability for voting outcomes, while making clear Consultant has no obligation to recommend either.
